concepts.name: Harshacharita: Nature, Authorship, and Literary Significance
key_dimensions: Authored by Banabhatta — court poet of Harsha; genre: biographical prose poetry (Akhyayika)
First biographical work in Sanskrit literature — distinction from Puranic hagiography
Reliability debate: panegyric vs. historical source — what it exaggerates vs. what it corroborates
Eight Uchchhvasas (chapters) and their coverage of Harsha's early life and accession

concepts.name: Xuanzang's Si-Yu-Ki: Nature, Purpose, and Historiographical Value
key_dimensions: Full title: 'Da Tang Xiyu Ji' (Great Tang Records on the Western Regions) — pilgrim's travelogue, not a political chronicle
Distinction between eyewitness accounts and hearsay in Xuanzang's narrative — UPSC trap on reliability
Comparison with Faxian's (Fa-Hien) account: socio-religious conditions then vs. Harsha's era
Role of Xuanzang's account in reconstructing Buddhist institutional history absent in Indian sources

concepts.name: Harsha's Accession and Political Legitimacy as Depicted in Harshacharita
key_dimensions: Circumstances of accession: death of brother Rajyavardhana at hands of Shashanka of Gauda
Role of sister Rajyashri's rescue and its political symbolism in legitimizing Harsha's claim
Banabhatta's portrayal of Harsha's reluctance to rule — literary trope vs. political reality
Harshacharita's silence on certain military defeats — what omissions reveal about source bias

concepts.name: Xuanzang's Description of Harsha's Administrative System
key_dimensions: Description of a decentralized polity with tributary chiefs — contrast with Gupta centralization
Revenue system: one-sixth tax on produce; three-quarter allocation to state functions vs. religion
Light taxation and its socio-economic implications as seen through Xuanzang's lens
Absence of harsh punishments (ordeal by water) — Xuanzang's observation vs. Arthashastra prescriptions

concepts.name: Shashanka of Gauda: Enemy of Harsha as Portrayed in Both Sources
key_dimensions: Harshacharita's depiction of Shashanka as villain responsible for Rajyavardhana's murder — partisan source
Xuanzang's account of Shashanka's persecution of Buddhism — uprooting of Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya
Historiographical problem: no Gauda source survives to counter-balance these accounts
Shashanka as the first independent ruler of Bengal — significance beyond Harsha's narrative

concepts.name: Xuanzang's Account of Buddhist Institutions: Nalanda and Monastic Economy
key_dimensions: Nalanda as a residential university — Xuanzang's detailed description of its curriculum, structure, and endowments
Royal patronage model: villages assigned to Nalanda for maintenance — proto-endowment system
Xuanzang's own stay and study at Nalanda — subjects studied (Yogachara, logic, Sanskrit)
Distinction Xuanzang draws between Mahayana and Hinayana centers — geographical spread across India

concepts.name: Kanauj Assembly (643 CE) as Described by Xuanzang
key_dimensions: Harsha's convening of a grand religious assembly at Kanauj — Xuanzang as eyewitness
Purpose: public debate on Mahayana doctrines, suggesting Harsha's religious orientation shift
Threatened violence by opponents — Xuanzang's account of the attack on Harsha and the fire
Political use of religious assembly: Kanauj as new imperial center replacing Pataliputra

concepts.name: Prayag (Allahabad) Quinquennial Assembly: Xuanzang's Account
key_dimensions: Xuanzang's description of the Mahamoksha Parishad held every five years at Prayag (Triveni Sangam)
Harsha's dana (charity) — distribution of accumulated treasury including personal clothing and jewelry
Religious pluralism: gifts to Buddhists, Brahmanas, Jains, and the poor — evidence of Harsha's syncretic policy
UPSC trap: Prayag assembly ≠ Kanauj assembly — different purposes, different years, different nature

concepts.name: Harsha's Religious Policy: Harshacharita vs. Xuanzang — Apparent Contradiction
key_dimensions: Harshacharita portrays Harsha's family as Shaiva — worship of Shiva prominent in early chapters
Xuanzang portrays Harsha as a devout Buddhist patron — apparent evolution or diplomatic pluralism
Resolution: Harsha practiced religious syncretism — coins show both Shaiva and Buddhist imagery
UPSC trap: neither source alone gives complete picture; using both sources to triangulate truth

concepts.name: Xuanzang's Socio-Economic Observations: Caste, Trade, and Urban Life
key_dimensions: Description of the caste system in practice — four varnas and outcastes (chandalas) living outside towns
Observation on merchants, guilds, and use of cowrie shells and gold coins in trade
Urban decline noted by Xuanzang compared to Faxian's account — shrinking cities, fewer wealthy merchants
Diet and food habits: Brahmanas, Kshatriyas avoiding beef; Buddhist monks' dietary rules

concepts.name: Harshacharita as a Source for Post-Gupta Political Geography
key_dimensions: References to kingdoms of the Deccan, Bengal (Gauda), and Punjab — mapping the political landscape
Description of Thanesar (Sthanvishvara) as Harsha's original kingdom — its location and significance
Mention of Malwa conflict and Northern India's fragmented polity after Gupta decline
Banabhatta's incidental references to forests, frontier regions — ecological and settlement history

concepts.name: Xuanzang's Account of the Decline of Buddhism in Parts of India
key_dimensions: Observation of ruined stupas and deserted monasteries in northwestern India — post-Hun devastation
Contrast between flourishing Buddhist centers in Bengal/Bihar vs. decline in Punjab and Sindh
Brahmanical resurgence noted indirectly — fewer Buddhist followers in certain regions
UPSC angle: Xuanzang's account as evidence for the beginning of Buddhist decline in India

concepts.name: Banabhatta's Portrayal of Society and Culture in Harshacharita
key_dimensions: Descriptions of forest dwellers, merchants, soldiers — cross-sectional social snapshot beyond elite
References to women's position: Rajyashri as an active political figure — agency vs. norm
Mention of Sati practice — one of earliest literary references; historiographical significance
Descriptions of art, music, and court culture — Harshacharita as a source for cultural history

concepts.name: Xuanzang and the Question of Harsha's Empire: Extent and Nature
key_dimensions: Xuanzang's claim that Harsha controlled 'Five Indias' — historiographical debate on its meaning
Pulakeshin II's defeat of Harsha on the Narmada — Xuanzang does NOT mention this; Aihole inscription does
UPSC trap: Xuanzang's account inflates Harsha's power — corroboration needed from epigraphy
Nature of Harsha's empire: imperial federation vs. centralized empire — evidence from both sources

concepts.name: Comparison of Faxian and Xuanzang Accounts: Gupta vs. Harsha Period India
key_dimensions: Faxian (399–414 CE): prosperous cities, thriving Buddhism, Chandala segregation — Gupta golden age
Xuanzang (629–645 CE): urban decline, political fragmentation, Buddhism under stress in some regions
Common themes: caste system, cow protection, role of Brahmanas — continuity across 200 years
UPSC trap: both are foreign Buddhist pilgrims — neither focuses on political economy as primary concern

concepts.name: Itsing (Yijing) vs. Xuanzang: Supplementary Chinese Sources on Post-Gupta Buddhism
key_dimensions: Yijing visited India (671–695 CE) — post-Harsha; describes Nalanda after Harsha's reign
Yijing's account corroborates Xuanzang on Nalanda's curriculum and monastic discipline
UPSC trap: Yijing is often confused with Xuanzang — different time periods, different political contexts
Yijing's account as evidence for continuity of Buddhist institutions after Harsha's death

concepts.name: Harshacharita's Account of Harsha's Military Campaigns and the Concept of Digvijaya
key_dimensions: Banabhatta describes Harsha's six-year campaign to subjugate northern India — literary vs. historical reading
Elephant corps and cavalry as primary military assets — Xuanzang also corroborates large elephant force
UPSC trap: Harshacharita covers only early campaigns; later military history (Narmada defeat) not in text
Concept of Digvijaya in post-Gupta context — Harsha as last great northern emperor before Rajput fragmentation

concepts.name: Source Criticism: Limitations and Biases of Harshacharita and Xuanzang Together
key_dimensions: Harshacharita: courtly bias, incomplete (covers only early life), Sanskrit literary conventions distort facts
Xuanzang: Buddhist bias, some regions visited vs. described from hearsay, Chinese translation layers
Methodological principle: neither source sufficient alone — need coins, inscriptions (Banskhera, Madhuban grants) for corroboration
UPSC angle: these are PRIMARY sources but not OBJECTIVE sources — distinguishing between the two is a key skill tested
